# 2 Maccabees Chapter 9 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic Equivalence)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 9 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_009_page_001.jpg

---

**9:1** Around this same time, Antiochus was being driven out of Persia in humiliating retreat.

**9:2** He had tried to loot the temple at Persepolis and take control of the city — but the citizens grabbed their weapons and fought back, and Antiochus was chased out in disgrace.

**9:3** He was in Ecbatana when the news caught up with him: Nicanor was dead, and Timothy's forces had been destroyed.

**9:4** The news threw him into a violent rage. He swore he would make the Jews pay for what had been done to him. He ordered his driver to push the horses without stopping, to make Jerusalem as fast as possible. "When I get there," he raved, "I'll turn Jerusalem into one mass grave." But God's justice was already riding alongside him.

**9:5** The Lord — the all-seeing God of Israel — struck him down with a hidden, incurable blow. Even as the words left his mouth, a savage, unrelenting pain ripped through his bowels and gripped his insides with torments he could not escape.

**9:6** A just punishment — he had ripped apart the insides of others with pain just as strange and severe.

**9:7** But he did not humble himself. If anything, his arrogance swelled. Seething with murderous rage against the Jews, he drove his men on. Then it happened: he was thrown from the chariot while it was moving at full speed, and slammed into the ground so hard that every joint in his body was wrenched.

**9:8** The man who had boasted that he could command the ocean waves and weigh mountains on a scale — that man was now being hauled around on a stretcher. The power of God was on full display.

**9:9** Worms began pouring out of his body. While he was still alive, his flesh rotted off him in agony and pain. The stench of his decaying body became so overwhelming that the whole army could not bear to come near him.

**9:10** Not long before, this was the man who had fancied he could touch the stars of heaven. Now no one could even stand to carry him, the smell was so unbearable.

**9:11** Then, finally, his spirit broke. God had beaten him down under the lash of pain, and moment by moment the arrogance drained out of him. He was being forced — the hard way — to see things clearly.

**9:12** When he could not endure even the smell of his own body, he said: "It is right to submit to God. A mortal man should not think himself the equal of God."

**9:13** Then this wretched man began making promises to the Lord — the Lord who would never again show him mercy:

**9:14** The holy city he had been racing to demolish and turn into a graveyard — he would grant it its freedom.

**9:15** The Jews he had planned to throw unburied to the birds and beasts, infants included — he would grant them the same rights as citizens of Athens.

**9:16** The holy temple he had looted — he would fill it with the finest offerings he could find. The sacred vessels he had stolen — he would return them multiplied many times over. He would personally fund the sacrifices out of his own treasury.

**9:17** On top of all this, he would convert to Judaism himself and travel the world proclaiming the greatness of God.

**9:18** None of it made any difference. His suffering did not let up for an instant — God's judgment had come down on him, and it was just. Having given up any hope of surviving, he wrote the following letter to the Jews. It was meant to read as a plea for mercy:

**9:19** "From Antiochus, king and general, to the worthy Jewish citizens: warmest greetings, wishes for good health, and every prosperity.

**9:20** I hope you and your children are well and that things are going as you wish. I give great thanks to God, whose help I depend on entirely.

**9:21** As for me — I am laid low with illness. But I remember with genuine warmth the respect and goodwill that existed between us. On my way back from Persia, struck by a stubborn sickness, I felt it was my responsibility to think about the welfare of all my subjects.

**9:22** I have not abandoned hope of recovery — I believe I will pull through —

**9:23** but I have seen how my own father, whenever he went on campaign in the eastern provinces, took care to name a successor,

**9:24** so that if anything unexpected happened, the people throughout the realm would know who was in charge and not fall into panic.

**9:25** I am also well aware that the neighboring princes are watching for any opening and waiting for their moment. I have therefore named my son Antiochus as king — a young man I have entrusted to many of you during my trips to the eastern provinces. I have written to him with my instructions.

**9:26** I urge and beg each of you to remember the benefits you have received, both publicly and personally, and to stay loyal to me and to my son.

**9:27** I trust he will deal with you with moderation and kindness, continuing the policy of goodwill I have always maintained toward you."

**9:28** That was the end of Antiochus the murderer and blasphemer — he died a wretched death, alone in the mountains of a foreign country, in exactly the kind of suffering he had inflicted on others.

**9:29** His foster brother Philip brought the body back. But afraid of what Antiochus's son might do to him, Philip fled to Ptolemy Philometor in Egypt.
